# A Comprehensive Survey on Interoperability for IIoT: Taxonomy, Standards, and Future Directions

Authors: Abhishek Hazra, Mainak Adhikari, Tarachand Amgoth, Satish Narayana Srirama Authors Info & Claims

Published: 23 November 2021 Publication History

Contents

### Abstract

In the era of Industry 4.0, the Internet-of-Things (IoT) performs the driving position analogous to the initial industrial metamorphosis. IoT affords the potential to couple machine-to-machine intercommunication and real-time information-gathering within the industry domain. Hence, the enactment of IoT in the industry magnifies effective optimization, authority, and data-driven judgment. However, this field undergoes several interoperable issues, including large numbers of heterogeneous IoT gadgets, tools, software, sensing, and processing components, joining through the Internet, despite the deficiency of communication protocols and standards. Recently, various interoperable protocols, platforms, standards, and technologies are enhanced and altered according to the specifications of the applicability in industrial applications. However, there are no recent survey papers that primarily examine various interoperability issues that Industrial IoT (IIoT) faces. In this review, we investigate the conventional and recent developments of relevant state-of-the-art IIoT technologies, frameworks, and solutions for facilitating interoperability between different IIoT components. We also discuss several interoperable IIoT standards, protocols, and models for digitizing the industrial revolution. Finally, we conclude this survey with an inherent discussion of open challenges and directions for future research.

## 1 Introduction

Recent advances in the Internet and its supported things in the existing world make the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) more reliable technology than ever before [139]. The term “ Internet of Things” was first used by Kevin Ashton, the British technology pioneer (1999, MIT Research), with his work with RFID tags. Specifically, IIoT connects a set of heterogeneous devices or things with unique identifications and standard communication, which makes a compatible interconnection between the IoT devices. The International Telecommunication Union (ITU) 1 defines the IoT as a “ global infrastructure for the information society, enabling advanced services by interconnecting (physical and virtual) things based on existing and evolving interoperable information and communication technologies.” The primary objectives of the IoT are communication between heterogeneous end-devices, sensing data through these devices, secure data storage at centralized servers, and finally, processing and transmitting the filtered information to the next level for controlling and monitoring the components of the network to improve the working condition of different personnel, reduce operational costs, and increase machines lifetime [138]. IIoT is empowering modern-day technologies through expanding the Internet competency to the sensing nodes and transmitting to the edge devices [8]. For example, with IIoT technology, farmers can track their real-time farming status, weather condition, and soil moisture conditions for improving the productivity of the crops. Doctors can monitor patients’ health conditions and give valuable suggestions in a 24/7 manner with a recommendation system for taking an emergency decision. Companies can predict the lifetimes of their devices/machines, track production processes, and efficiently utilize human resources. Thus, IIoT technology is an emerging era for handling real-time applications in a complex environment.

Complexity pervasive systems are superseded by the traditional view of homogeneous distributed systems, where the domain-specific IIoT applications, including smart transportation, smart city, agriculture, smart health-care, 2 smart water, and waste management are individually designed and developed upon domain-specific platforms and middleware [28]. Moreover, these technology-dependent IIoT devices are composed and connected with various computing devices to create an efficient and richer interconnected dynamic structure. There are various challenging issues in the field of IIoT application, a central one is “ interoperability,” i.e., the ability to connect one or more IIoT devices and understand and exchange data with one another for a given purpose [143]. However, building an interoperable IIoT enabling technology entirely depends on the various IIoT devices and their functionalists in the industrial environment [28]. There are two key properties for dealing with the interoperability issue in the IIoT domain: extreme heterogeneity and dynamic and spontaneous communication.

Extreme heterogeneity: The IIoT devices, including smart industrial devices, smart sensors, and actuators are connected using networking, middleware, and application-based protocols with different data types. Each of the IIoT devices can be seen to add a plethora of technologies, causing problems with device understandability during data transmission and processing. Moreover, device type, processing capability, associated technology, and device functionality encourage extreme heterogeneity in the IIoT domain.

Dynamic and spontaneous communication: The connection between the IIoT devices are not made until run-time, i.e., no design or deployment decision can inform the interoperability solution [46].

Current researches, including References [9, 86], show that IIoT solutions are widely adopted for a broad range of industrial applications (e.g., automation, predictive maintenance, and smart logistics) from the last decades and a large number of small industries and start-ups are also breeding over this period. Therefore, each organization started providing its infrastructure, proprietary protocols, standards, Application Programming Interfaces (APIs), and data formats that are not standardized globally and cannot carry out an interoperable issue in the IIoT domain [70]. From the end-users point of view, interoperability issues are also leading to unsolvable problems, such as vendor lock-in, where the customers get stuck with a specific vendor due to un-interoperable communication between vendors and non-standardized architecture on cross-platform [74]. Hence, adding a non-interoperable solution to a standard industrial ecosystem and, finally, creating a barrier to the development is one of the critical open research challenges in the IIoT [97].

### 1.1 Scope of Survey

With the dominant demand for Industry 4.0 and its complementary technologies, a large number of heterogeneous devices are connecting every day, despite standardized protocols and interoperable architecture. These devices (e.g., large size healthcare devices, industrial machinery robots, and small-sized sensors and actuators) continuously generate thousands of terabytes of data per second for processing or analysis. Thus, heterogeneity comes not only from data/device but also from various levels of industrial architecture, and interoperability is the center point of all such complicated issues. The main research questions regarding the interoperable IIoT ecosystem are:

(1)

Why is interoperability an important aspect of the industrial revolution?

(2)

What are the various interoperability issues that the industry are facing?

(3)

What are the current interoperable architecture, protocols, and standards for large-scale IIoT deployment?

(4)

Do Industry 4.0 technologies address global interoperability issues for the industrial revolution?

This study aims at enhancing digitization and standardization within the paradigm of Industry 4.0. In this survey, we conduct a comprehensive literature review on various aspects of interoperability issues and state-of-the-art Industry 4.0 solutions from four significant interoperability dimensions, including technology, revolution, protocol and standard, and architecture. This survey emphasizes various interoperable architectures, protocols, and standards related to IoT and IIoT domains, and it discusses several open research challenges related to the interoperable framework. Besides that, we also explore basic interoperability patterns, several core interoperability issues, and a guide for handling those issues to obtain an interoperable industrial ecosystem. This article goes beyond the available studies and specifically focuses mostly on the intersection between Industry 4.0 and IIoT interoperability research directions.

### 1.2 Related Work

In this work, we led a comprehensive literature inspection by reviewing associated articles from six important scholastic databases (ACM digital library, Web of Knowledge, IEEE Xplore, Web of Knowledge, Google Scholar, and ScienceDirect) to understand the current research status and prospects of IoT in industry. During the literature review, we have observed that a large number of conference papers and journal articles have been published since 2015 in the domains of “ IoT,” “ IIoT,” “ Industry 4.0,” and “ Interoperability.” Specifically, we have deeply analyzed and surveyed the past five years of works, including review papers, technical journals, and high-quality conference papers, which provide foremost perceptions on interoperability issues of IoT-IIoT-Industry 4.0 and make the review much more manageable while satisfying research questions, defined in Section 1.1. Besides that, we have commonly excluded articles that were published more than five years ago, especially conference and editorial board articles.

From Figure 1(a), it can be observed that most of the interoperability issues have been addressed for the IoT environment. Specifically, 54% of the total researches have been done only for the IoT domain; however, 24% of researches are related to IIoT, and the remaining 22% of the works are on Industry 4.0, which suggests that there needs to be more focus on IIoT and Industry 4.0 solutions to establish an interoperable ecosystem. From the interoperability perspective, shown in Figure 1(b), a considerable amount of works are found for technical interoperability (36%) and semantic interoperability (23%). Moreover, the average number of works have been considered for pragmatic interoperability (16%) and platform interoperability (13%) by the researchers. However, two low-interest areas are also found near conceptual and syntactic interoperability. Only a negligible amount of works have been done for these two domains, with 7% and 5% of research efforts, respectively, which also reflects that more there needs to be more attention focused on these two domains.
